Learning Objectives
Recognize patient populations and risk factors associated with osteoporosis.
Identify indications and diagnostic pathways for bone health assessment.
Specify the principles and treatment options for optimizing bone health in patients with a
history of osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures.
Determine the appropriate evaluation and treatment options for osteoporotic vertebral
compression fractures.

Bone Remodeling
Is a balance between osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and osteoblastic bone formation
Uncoupling between osteoblast and osteoclast function results in metabolic bone disease,
leading to decreased bone mineral density (BMD) and inferior bone quality.

Introduction
Bone progresses through a constant process of recycling to accommodate varying
mechanical stresses, repair small portions of damage, and facilitate systemic calcium
homeostasis.1 This process is influenced by mechanical forces (Wolff’s law) and the
endocrine system, with signals such as parathyroid hormone, thyroid hormones,
glucocorticoids, and growth hormone playing an influential role. Patients with altered
hormonal states, such as Cushing syndrome, may present with osteopenia or
osteoporosis at an early age.2
Definitions
Osteopenia and osteoporosis are bone quantity problems related to an insufficient amount of
normal bone (Figure 1; Resource 1).
Osteomalacia is a bone quality problem related to abnormal/inadequate mineralization of
osteoid matrix.
Most commonly the result of vitamin D deficiency
May lead to skeletal pain and fracture

Osteoporosis Epidemiology
Osteoporosis is most common in females and is strongly correlated with age.
Fragility fractures are common, and their incidence generally increases over time.

Osteoporosis Epidemiology
An estimated 10.3% of the US population has osteoporosis, and almost one-half (43%) of
the US population has osteopenia.3 Osteoporosis is associated with advancing age,
occurring in 5% of individuals aged 50 to 59 years, 8% of individuals aged 60 to 69 years,
16.4% of individuals aged 70 to 79 years, and 26.2% in individuals 80 years and older.3 In

addition, women are three times more likely than men to have osteoporosis.
Approximately 1.5 million Americans sustain a low-energy fragility fracture each year,
with 700,000 of these injuries occurring in the spine.4 Because patients are living longer
and the prevalence of osteoporosis is associated with age, an increase in the number of
these injuries each year is anticipated.
Classification of Osteoporosis
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is the preferred imaging modality for assessing BMD
(Figure 2).
Measures areal BMD (gm/cm2) in regions of interest, including the femoral neck, total hip,
lumbar spine (L1 through L4), and one-third distal radius. Arthritis of the spine may falsely
elevate bone density; therefore, particular attention should be paid to T-scores in the femoral
neck and the one-third distal radius.
Indications for DEXA
The T-score is the number of standard deviations from a reference of BMD values from
young healthy females.
Value used for the diagnosis of osteoporosis
The Z-score is the number of standard deviations from a reference for age- and gender-
matched subjects.
World Health Organization classification based on BMD derived from DEXA (Table 1)

The lowest T-score of the femoral neck, total proximal femur, L1 through L4, or one-third distal
radius is used to classify bone status.
Osteoporosis is diagnosed if a T-score is less than or equal to −2.5 (ie, 2.5 standard deviations
from the mean of a BMD from a population of young, healthy females).
Osteopenia is diagnosed if a T-score is −1.0 to −2.5 (ie, 1 to 2.5 standard deviations from the
mean of a BMD from a population of young, healthy females).
The risk of osteoporotic fragility fractures is strongly associated with higher T-scores.5
Updated classification includes patient history or presence of a fragility fracture and decreased
BMD.


Classification of Osteoporosis
Although BMD measurement provides an objective measure of osteoporosis, sole
implementation of widely accepted cutoff values to diagnose osteoporosis does not
appropriately identify all patients who are candidates for treatment.6 Therefore, because
osteoporosis is associated with an increased risk for fragility fractures (and morbidity of
these injuries), the National Bone Health Alliance has suggested consideration of other
objective criteria in assessing a patient’s metabolic bone health.7 This expands the
diagnosis of osteoporosis to patients who already have an increased risk of fragility
fractures but who would otherwise not be considered for medical treatment if BMD were
the only criterion to initiate treatment.
The FRAX is a free, online clinical tool that assists in identifying patients who may benefit
from prevention of primary and secondary factors or treatment, using a series of known
risk factors (including, but not limited to BMD; Table 3).8
The FRAX guidelines suggest medical treatment of postmenopausal females and males
older than 50 years who meet any of the following criteria: a hip or vertebral fragility
fracture, a T-score less than −2.5 (osteoporosis), a T-score between −1.0 and −2.5
(osteopenia), a 10-year hip fracture risk greater than or equal to 3%, and a 10-year major
osteoporotic fracture risk greater than or equal to20%. In addition, the FRAX tool also
can identify patients in whom a DEXA scan is indicated.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Diagnosis of Osteoporosis

Diagnosis of Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is diagnosed if BMD is less than −2.5. Because many patients with a BMD
greater than −2.5 are at risk for fragility fractures, studies have suggested that the
definition of osteoporosis consider more than only DEXA results.9 The presence or
history of a fragility fracture should be considered because patients who present with
this injury have demonstrated inferior bone quality independent of DEXA results.

Patient History
Consider bone health in evaluating all orthopaedic patients.
Identify risk factors.
Use available imaging studies, such as old DEXA or opportunistic CT.
Order DEXA if indicated.

Patient History
Bone quality dictates the success or failure of orthopaedic surgical management and, if
not appropriately optimized and managed, patients may have an increased risk for
fracture. Therefore, bone quality must be considered in the treatment of all orthopaedic
patients. Risk factors for poor bone health and indications for ordering a DEXA scan are
summarized in Table 4.
Table 4

Imaging Studies
Opportunistic CT imaging
DEXA is the preferred imaging modality to assess BMD.
Vertebral fracture assessment

Imaging Studies
Although CT scans should not be ordered specifically to evaluate a patient’s bone quality,
they often are available and allow for estimation of the patient’s BMD.10 CT is based on
an attenuation coefficient called the Hounsfield unit, which measures the attenuation
coefficient of tissue.11 Examples of measurements include air (-1000 Hounsfield unit),
water (0 Hounsfield unit), and bone (positive Hounsfield unit value that varies with
density). Because the Hounsfield unit value is related to BMD, it can be used to estimate
BMD and the presence of osteoporosis. L1 vertebral body thresholds of less than 135
Hounsfield unit in an axial view are associated with osteoporosis.12
This technique uses DEXA imaging data to identify vertebral fractures and is associated
with strong concordance with plain radiographs.13 Patients with osteopenia and a
history or current diagnosis of a fragility fracture are considered to have osteoporosis.
Therefore, vertebral fracture assessment may inform treatment decisions because the
recommendations for osteoporosis management are different than the
recommendations for osteopenia.
Management
Principles and Management of Bone Health

Dietary considerations14
Optimize daily protein intake in malnourished patients (1.0 to 1.2 g/kg of body weight).
Ensure adequate vitamin D and calcium intake.
Exercise
Weight-bearing exercises promote osteoblastic function and are essential to maintain bone
stock.
Ask about falls, which are a substantial risk factor for subsequent fracture.
Assess gait and ability to get up from a chair and take three steps.
If necessary, consider physical therapy for strength training, balance, and fall prevention.
Patients with history of falls at home should consider home physical therapy visits to
optimize living conditions with the goal to avoid additional falls.
Substance/medication modifications
Encourage discontinuation of smoking and excess alcohol.
Limit caffeinated beverages to 1 to 2 U/day.

Principles and Management of Bone Health
Vitamin D optimizes bone health by promoting calcium absorption and osteoblast
differentiation and mineralization and by enhancing collagen cross-linking. Vitamin D is
available in several food sources, and the liver and kidneys are involved in conversion of
7-dehydrocholesterol into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Serum assays
measure 25-dihydroxyvitamin D (the inactive form), the most abundant metabolite.
Recommended levels continue to be a subject of controversy. The American Association
of Clinical Endocrinology 25-dihydroxyvitamin D recommendations are shown in Table 5.
Daily calcium recommendations are 1 g for younger females and males and 1.2 g for
postmenopausal females.
BMD is a product of systemic endocrine signaling and biomechanical stresses; therefore,
optimize the available substrates with appropriate dietary protein and calcium,
supplement with vitamin D if indicated, and promote weight-bearing activity. These
general principles are not optimal treatment options for patients diagnosed with
osteoporosis who are candidates for antiresorptive or anabolic medical therapy.

Disadvantages are high cost and occasional hypercalcemia.


Medical Management of Osteoporosis

The medical treatment guidelines for patients with osteoporosis are oriented to prevent
primary or secondary fragility fractures. Treatment for all patients at risk for
osteopenia/osteoporosis includes baseline bone health optimization and
antiresorptive/anabolic therapies. The choice of antiresorptive or anabolic agent is best
left to a specialist familiar with safe and effective dosing regimens and potential adverse
effects. Collaboration with a dedicated fracture liaison who optimizes medical regimens
and increases the delivery of such care to at-risk patients is recommended.
Preoperative Bone-health Optimization for Spine Patients
Bone-health optimization is a potential modifiable risk factor to improve outcomes and
prevent complications in patients undergoing elective spine surgery.
Preoperative bone-health optimization assessment and treatment are recommended in
patients older than 50 years undergoing thoracolumbar surgery.
Antiosteoporosis medications improve elective spine surgery outcomes.
Metabolic bone and endocrine abnormalities are associated with fracture nonunion and
delayed union.

Preoperative Bone-health Optimization for Spine Patients
All patients older than 50 years should be screened for risk factors of osteoporosis
because approximately 50% of patients in this demographic seeking elective spine
surgery have low bone mass or osteoporosis.23 Poor bone health is associated with
subsidence of cages, pedicle screw loosening, proximal junction failure, poorer fusion
rates, increased spondylolisthesis after laminectomy, and higher rates of revision
surgery. Bjerke et al24 reviewed 140 patients who underwent lumbar fusion and found
that 10 patients (7%) had osteoporosis and 82 patients (59%) had low bone mass. In this
study, nonunion was reported in 50% of patients with osteoporosis versus 18% of
patients with low bone mass or a normal BMD. Osteoporotic-related complications
occurred in 23% of patients with normal BMD, 28% of patients with low bone mass, and
46% of patents with osteoporosis. Complication rates were poor relative to BMD if more
than single-level fusion was performed.

Vitamin D deficiency has been reported in 75% of patients who undergo elective spine
surgery.25,26 Studies have demonstrated slower fusion and lower success rates in
vitamin D–deficient patients.27 Other studies suggest that a low baseline vitamin D level
is associated with poorer postoperative Oswestry Low Back Disability Questionnaire
scores.28
Because of the substantial detriments associated with osteoporosis and elective spine
surgery, the American Orthopaedic Association suggests adopting the same principles as
those outlined for secondary fracture prevention.29 These principles should be
considered for all patients older than 50 years who are undergoing thoracolumbar
surgery (Table 5; Resource 2).
Patients who do not require DEXA or who have a negative DEXA scan should undergo
surgical treatment without additional workup or treatment for osteoporosis.
Preoperative bone health optimization,30 including diphosphonate or anabolic agents
(preference of the authors of this lesson) should be considered in patients who have
low-bone-mass osteoporosis. The duration of preoperative treatment varies; however,
effects on bone strength and physiology generally are observed within 2 months;
therefore the authors recommend beginning management a minimum of 3 months
preoperatively, if clinically possible. For multilevel or high-risk (osteotomy) procedures,
longer management (as long as 9 months) should be considered.
Multiple randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing diphosphonates and a placebo in
patients undergoing lumbar spine fusion reported improved clinical and radiographic
outcomes and a lower risk of complications.31 In addition, diphosphonates are not
associated with any impairment of bone healing.32 A RCT and multiple cohort studies
showed that teriparatide may lead to improved clinical and radiographic outcomes and a
lower risk of complications in patients undergoing spinal fusoin.33
Successful fracture union or fusion may be affected by several factors, including
infection, stability, nicotine use, malnutrition, vitamin deficiency, prematurely loading the
fracture/fusion site, and metabolic/endocrine irregularities. In a 2007 case series, 37
trauma patients without other risk factors for nonunion were referred to an

endocrinology service for evaluation of metabolic etiologies.34 Thirty-one patients
(83.8%) had metabolic or other endocrine conditions, including calcium imbalances,
hypogonadism, thyroid and parathyroid conditions, and vitamin D deficiency. Eight of
these patients achieved successful fracture union after medical treatment of the
underlying hormone/metabolic issue. Another retrospective review reported that
trauma patients with an upper or lower extremity fracture who did not have an initial
vitamin D deficiency had a 0.3% delayed union rate.35 Patients with a vitamin D
deficiency who responded to supplementation had a 1.7% delayed union rate. Vitamin
D­–deficient patients who did not respond to supplementation had a substantially higher
delayed union rate (9.7%). Overall, osteoporosis is a common risk factor for fragility
fractures and increased surgical complications; however, other metabolic conditions
may have a considerable effect on bone health.
Secondary Fracture Prevention
A history of fragility fracture is a substantial risk factor for subsequent fracture.
Considerable evidence demonstrates poor adherence to established protocols for the medical
management of osteoporosis after a fragility fracture.
Medical management of osteoporosis may substantially decrease the incidence of secondary
fractures.
Increased awareness of the need for medical management after any fragility fracture and the
implementation of fracture prevention programs (fracture liaison service) may improve patient
outcomes.

Secondary Fracture Prevention
A Medicare retrospective cohort study reported a cumulative risk of subsequent fragility
fractures of 10%, 18%, and 31% at 1 year, 2 years, and 5 years, respectively, if medical
management is not initiated.36 Therefore, the goal of management after an osteoporotic
vertebral compression fracture is to prevent the next one. Fewer than 30% of patients
with a vertebral compression fracture undergo appropriate osteoporotic medical
treatment within 1 year (Resource 3). Another study found adherence to established

AAOS | Osteoporotic Vertebral Compression Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001079
16/30

guidelines for medical management of osteoporosis after fragility fractures in 33% of
female patients and 17% of male patients.37
In a database analysis, secondary treatment was provided in 10% of patients diagnosed
with any fragility fracture but was associated with a 25% overall risk reduction in all
fragility fractures.38 The Own the Bone program was developed by the American
Orthopaedic Association to encourage orthopaedic surgeons to take ownership of bone
health after a fragility fracture. The program has been implemented at 150 sites in all
states in the United States and substantially improves compliance with treatment
recommissions after fragility fracture.39 Dedicated bone-health services also can
improve patient outcomes by developing and implementing comprehensive bone-health
programs.
Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures
Areas within the skeletal system with a high concentration of trabecular bone, such as the
vertebral bodies of the thoracic and lumbar spine, are prone to fracture.
Osteoporotic vertebral fractures are common injuries but most are asymptomatic.
Symptomatic injuries are associated with considerable morbidity.

Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures
Cancellous bone has a much higher surface area compared with cortical bone and
undergoes a higher rate of remodeling. Because osteoporosis arises from a pathologic
disturbance between the osteoclast-osteoblast remodeling mechanism, areas of the
skeletal system with a higher density of cancellous bone are more compromised in
patients with osteoporosis. These include the distal radius, the intertrochanteric region
of the proximal femur, the proximal humerus, and the vertebral bodies of the thoracic
and lumbar spine. In addition, as patients age, a more positive sagittal balance tends to
occur in which the trunk migrates more anteriorly in relation to the pelvis. This increase
in kyphosis creates a longer lever arm over the thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies and

level falls (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustrations show progressive spinal deformity associated with osteoporosis.
Compression fractures of thoracic vertebrae lead to loss of height and progressive
thoracic kyphosis (dowager hump). The lower ribs eventually rest on the iliac crests, and
downward pressure on the viscera causes abdominal distention. (Reproduced from
Griffin LY: Osteoporosis, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal
Care 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 156-165.)
Approximately 600,000 to 800,000 vertebral compression fractures occur each year in
United States;4 however, only one-third are clinically symptomatic.40
A substantial reduction in quality-adjusted life years was found in females with a
vertebral compression fracture compared with age-adjusted control patients (0.63

53.9%, 30.9%, and 10.5% at 3 years, 5 years, and 7 years postinjury, respectively.43
Diagnosis of Vertebral Fractures
Patients commonly describe a low-energy mechanism of injury, such as a fall from standing
height.
The diagnosis typically is made on plain radiographs or CT scans (Figure 4); however, it also
can be made via vertebral fracture assessment.
Figure 4 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of a spine show an L2 compression fracture.

Classification of vertebral fracture
Genant classification is most commonly used.
Grade 1: mild (<25%) height loss
Grade 2: moderate (25% to 40%) height loss
Grade 3: severe (>40%) height loss
Most providers consider only moderate and severe injuries as clinical important.
This classification system does not include burst-type injuries with involvement of the
vertebral endplates and the posterior vertebral wall.

Diagnosis of Vertebral Fractures
Vertebral compression injuries typically present as a loss of vertebral height at the
affected level and may increase kyphotic alignment of the thoracolumbar spine. An acute
measured height change of more than 2 cm is suggestive of acute vertebral fracture. If
age determination is required, MRI can show edema in the vertebral body, which
appears as an enhanced signal on T2-weighted images, indicating recent fracture (Figure
5). Associated neurological injury is uncommon, and the posterior elements rarely are
involved. (Resource 4)

Most vertebral compression fractures can be managed nonsurgically.
Bracing often is poorly tolerated and has not been demonstrated to substantially improve
outcomes.

Management of Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures
Management generally consists of early mobilization with physical therapy and pain
control. Opioid pain medications should be minimized because of the pronounced
adverse effects of opiate pain medications in elderly patients. Instead, a multimodal
opioid-sparing pain regimen, including a muscle relaxer, neuroleptic agent (gabapentin
or pregabalin), acetaminophen, anti-inflammatory medication, topical analgesic agent
(lidocaine patch), and ice, should be used as tolerated. Bracing management for comfort
often is poorly tolerated in elderly patients. A RCT investigating the role of bracing in
patients with osteoporotic compression fractures demonstrated no difference in pain
relief, functional outcomes, and radiographic parameters.44 Serial upright radiographs
to monitor vertebral collapse or increased deformity may be indicated if pain does not
resolve within the expected timeframe. Most patients can be successfully treated
nonsurgically; however, cement augmentation or surgical stabilization may be indicated
in patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails. All patients with a vertebral fragility
fracture should be assessed and treated for osteoporosis to prevent subsequent
fracture.
Cement Augmentation
Vertebroplasty is a procedure in which cement is introduced into the vertebral body via a
transpedicular route without attempting to restore vertebral body height.
Kyphoplasty is a procedure that uses a balloon impactor to restore vertebral height before
cement augmentation, also via a transpedicular route (Figure 6).

Indications for cement augmentation
Failed 2- to 3-week trial of nonsurgical management and poor patient mobility or pain control
requiring a large amount of opioids
Increased collapse or worsening clinical deformity45
Nonunion or fracture cleft in vertebral body
Acute or subacute findings on short tau inversion recovery MRI with associated edema
Contraindications
Burst-type fractures
History or possibility of infection
Conflicting results of vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty.
Multiple RCTs comparing nonsurgical management with cement augmentation show
improved pain relief and function in treatment groups.46

Two sham-controlled RCTs do not show benefit.47,48
Database and registry studies show rapid improvement and lower mortality with cement
augmentation.42,49
Outcomes of adjacent-level fractures are no different between cement augmentation and
nonsurgically treated groups.50
Surgical Management of Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures
Instrumentation across the fracture rarely is warranted secondary to medical risks and
hardware-related complications.
If surgical management is selected, well-defined goals should guide approach and procedure
selection.

Surgical Management of Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures
Surgical procedures in patients with osteoporosis are associated with a higher
complication rate. Specific examples include cage subsidence, loosening of pedicle
screws, proximal junction failure, inferior fusion rates, and higher rates of revision
surgery.24 Indications for surgical management of osteoporotic compression fractures
include neurologic deterioration from retropulsed fragments or severe kyphotic
deformity, considerable and progressive deformity, failure of cement augmentation to
relieve symptoms, and exacerbation of spinal stenosis. Surgical treatment goals may
include decompression, stabilization, and deformity correction, depending on the needs
of the patient. Surgical outcomes in patients with an osteoporotic compression fracture
are relatively poor given the complexity of surgical treatment, patient age, associated
comorbidities, and the presence of poor bone quality.
Conclusion
Poor bone health predisposes patients to vertebral compression fractures, which are
associated with high mortality and morbidity risks.
Secondary fracture prevention is critical in patients with a vertebral compression fracture.

Osteoporosis and vitamin D deficiency are common and associated with poorer outcomes,
recurrent fractures, and higher complication risks.
Management using evidence-based protocols is desirable and can be accomplished via
programs such as fracture liaison services or referral to bone health specialists.
Spine practitioners should understand how to assess bone health, order and interpret DEXA
scans, and ensure patients are properly evaluated.
Spine practitioners should understand antiosteoporosis medications so they can properly
counsel patients.
Vertebral compression fractures typically are managed nonsurgically. If surgical treatment is
considered in osteoporotic patients, the goals of the procedure and the limitations of
instrumentation need to be clearly delineated.
Consider bone-health assessment in all patients undergoing thoracolumbar spine surgery or
patients with a fracture who are older than 50 years.
